items.rationale: Picking a side in advance (a keeper-independent strategy) means choosing the target before the run-up and committing to it, so all attention goes to technique. Option a describes the keeper-dependent strategy.

When the keeper commits early, watching gives you real information, so you can aim away from the dive. Research on penalty kicks (van der Kamp, 2006) found the keeper-dependent approach is advantageous mainly when the keeper commits early. Option b ignores that information.

A keeper who waits gives you nothing to read before you must commit your kicking action, so watching adds cost and no benefit; picking a corner in advance is better. Option a shows M3, the belief that you can always read the keeper in time.

items.answer: There is too little time to change the kicking action, so accuracy and power suffer.
accepted: Not enough time to change the kick, so the shot gets worse
Late changes to your aim disrupt your technique and make the shot less accurate
You have little time to adjust, which hurts the quality of the kick
Less accurate shot because there is not enough time to adjust
items.rationale: Changing aim late leaves insufficient time to modify the kicking action, which degrades the strike (van der Kamp, 2006). A response that says watching 'costs nothing' shows M3.

Committing to a corner first and striking it with a controlled swing matches the mission: placement in the corner with enough power. Option a repeats M2 and M1 (planting behind the ball, power over placement). Option c mixes the two strategies and loses the benefit of committing.

items.answer: The keeper may guess or dive to your side, and you cannot adjust once you have committed.
accepted: The keeper might go the same way and you can't change
You can't adapt if the keeper guesses your side
The keeper could save it because you ignore what the keeper does
If the keeper picks the same side, you cannot change your shot
items.rationale: Committing means you cannot use what the keeper does, so a keeper who guesses your side, or who stays central and saves a weak shot, beats you. The trade-off: picking in advance protects technique, and watching gains information but costs time.
